items.prompt: What are Git's three areas for tracking a file's state?
choices: Local, remote, and cloud
Working tree (files on disk), staging area/index (prepared for next commit), and repository (committed history)
HEAD, branch, and tag
Origin, upstream, and fork
items.explanation: Git separates a file's current on-disk state, its staged-for-next-commit snapshot, and its permanently committed history into three distinct areas — this is the model git status reports against.
items.reference:
AreaUpdated by
Working treeEditing files
Staging/indexgit add

Why: a file can be in a different state in all three areas at once.
items.learnMore:
Three areas, not one

Most confusion about 'where did my change go' traces back to conflating these three areas into one mental 'the file.' Git status exists specifically to report the differences between them.

Common mistake

Assuming 'I edited the file' is the same as 'the file is staged' or 'the file is committed' — all three are genuinely different states.

items.prompt: What moves a file's content from the staging area into the repository?
choices: `git add`
`git commit`
`git checkout`
Simply saving the file in your editor
items.explanation: `git commit` takes whatever is currently staged (in the index) and permanently records it as a new commit in the repository's history.

`git add`
`git checkout`
`git log`
items.explanation: `git add` moves a file's current content into the staging area/index — a prepared snapshot for the NEXT commit, not a permanent record on its own.

items.prompt: A developer edits a file on `feature-a` without committing, then switches to `feature-b`. Is the edit "tied to" feature-a?
choices: Yes — uncommitted edits always stay on the branch where they were made
No — uncommitted edits live in the working tree, which has no branch affinity; a branch is just a name pointing at a commit
Only if the file was staged with `git add` first
It depends on the file extension
items.explanation: A branch is a pointer to a commit — nothing more. Since the edit was never committed, it isn't part of any commit, and therefore isn't 'on' any branch at all; it's just sitting in the shared working tree.
items.reference:
Assumption: "my edit belongs to feature-a"

Reality: the edit belongs to nothing — it was never committed anywhere

Why: branches point at commits; uncommitted work isn't in any commit yet.
items.learnMore:
Branches are pointers, not containers

A branch doesn't 'hold' files the way a folder holds files — it's a lightweight, movable pointer to a single commit. Uncommitted work exists in the working tree/index, which Git updates on checkout, but doesn't itself belong to any branch.

Common mistake

Thinking of a branch like a folder that contains your in-progress work — it only contains what's been committed.

items.prompt: Why does an uncommitted edit sometimes 'follow' you silently when you switch branches?
choices: Git always copies uncommitted edits to every branch automatically

`checkout` only updates files that differ between the current and target commit — if the file is identical on both branches, checkout leaves the working tree copy (including any uncommitted edit) untouched
It's a bug that was never fixed
It only happens if you use `git switch` instead of `git checkout`
items.explanation: Checkout compares each file between the two commits being switched between — if there's no difference, there's nothing for checkout to update, so whatever is sitting in the working tree (edited or not) stays exactly as it is.

items.prompt: What is a Git branch, technically?
choices: A folder containing a copy of every file for that line of work
A lightweight, movable pointer to a single commit
A permanent snapshot of the entire working tree at a point in time
A special kind of remote server
items.explanation: A branch is just a named pointer to a commit — this is why uncommitted work (which isn't part of any commit) has no inherent connection to whichever branch happens to be checked out.

items.prompt: When does `git checkout <branch>` refuse to switch, protecting you from a silent loss?
choices: Never — checkout always switches branches unconditionally
When a file has both uncommitted changes AND genuinely differs between the current and target branch's commits, in a way that can't be cleanly merged
Whenever you have any uncommitted changes at all, regardless of the target branch
Only when using `git switch`, never with `git checkout`
items.explanation: Git only refuses when proceeding would risk losing or corrupting uncommitted work — specifically when the file both has uncommitted changes and genuinely differs on the target branch. If the file is identical between branches, there's nothing to protect against, so it proceeds silently instead.
items.reference:
error: Your local changes ... would be overwritten by checkout

Why: this only fires when the file genuinely diverged AND has uncommitted changes.
items.learnMore:
The protected case vs. the silent case

Counterintuitively, the case where checkout refuses (files genuinely diverged) is the SAFER one — you get an explicit warning. The case where it proceeds silently (files identical) is the one that can quietly set up a later loss, because nothing marks the file as having 'foreign' uncommitted content.

Common mistake

Assuming a clean, warning-free checkout means nothing risky is happening — it can still leave at-risk uncommitted work sitting somewhere easy to forget about.

items.prompt: Which scenario is actually SAFER: checkout refusing with an error, or checkout succeeding silently?
choices: Checkout succeeding silently is always safer, since it means no errors occurred
Checkout refusing is safer — it gives an explicit warning before anything risky happens, unlike a silent success which can quietly set up a later loss
They're equally safe in all cases
Neither is safe; both should be avoided entirely
items.explanation: A refused checkout stops you and tells you exactly what's at risk. A silent, successful checkout gives no such warning — the uncommitted edit is safe for now, but nothing marks it as 'foreign' content on the new branch, which is exactly what set up L3's incident.
items.reference:
error: Your local changes ... would be overwritten by checkout

Why: this only fires when the file genuinely diverged AND has uncommitted changes.

Common mistake

Assuming a clean, warning-free checkout means nothing risky is happening — it can still leave at-risk uncommitted work sitting somewhere easy to forget about.

items.prompt: `git status` shows a file under both "changes to be committed" AND "changes not staged for commit" at the same time. What does that mean?
choices: This is a Git error and should never happen

The file's staged version differs from HEAD (index vs. HEAD diff), AND the working tree version differs from what's staged (working tree vs. index diff) — the file has been edited twice, once staged and once not
It means the file was deleted
It means the file is untracked
items.explanation: git status runs two independent diffs. A file can differ in both comparisons at once: staged content differs from the last commit (staged changes), AND the current on-disk content differs from what's staged (additional unstaged edits on top).
items.reference:
"changes to be committed" = index vs. HEAD diff

"changes not staged for commit" = working tree vs. index diff

Why: these are two SEPARATE diffs — a file can appear in both simultaneously.
items.learnMore:
Two diffs, one status report

This is the concrete mechanism behind git status's output categories — understanding them as two separate diffs (not one combined 'is it changed' check) explains every category status can print, including the double-edit case.

Common mistake

Running `git add` once and assuming the file is now fully captured — any further edit after that `add` creates a new, separate unstaged diff.

items.prompt: A file shows only "changes not staged for commit" — nothing under "changes to be committed." What does this tell you about its staged version?
choices: The staged version matches the last commit exactly (no index vs. HEAD diff), but the working tree has since been edited beyond that
The file has never been committed
The file was deleted from the index
This combination is impossible
items.explanation: Only the working-tree-vs-index diff is showing a difference — meaning the index still matches HEAD exactly, and all the new edits exist only in the working tree, not yet staged.
items.reference:

"changes not staged for commit" = working tree vs. index diff

Why: these are two SEPARATE diffs — a file can appear in both simultaneously.

items.prompt: You `git add` a file, then edit it again before committing. What does `git commit` (without `-a` or a second `git add`) actually record?
choices: The latest on-disk version, including the second edit
Whatever was staged at the time of `git add` — the second edit, made after staging, is NOT included, since commit snapshots the index, not the working tree
Both versions, as two separate commits
Nothing — Git refuses to commit if the working tree differs from the index
items.explanation: git commit snapshots whatever is currently in the INDEX, not the working tree. An edit made after `git add` but before `git commit` is not captured unless it's staged again — this is a very common source of 'why isn't my latest change in this commit.'

items.prompt: Per-file, what's the FIRST question checkout effectively asks when switching branches?
choices: Does the working tree have any uncommitted changes at all, anywhere in the repo?
Does this specific file's content differ between the current commit and the target commit?
Is the file larger than a certain size?
Has the file ever been renamed?
items.explanation: Checkout evaluates each file independently: if the file's content is identical between the current and target commits, there's nothing to reconcile, and any uncommitted edit to that file is left completely alone.
items.reference:
1. Does the file differ between commits?

2. If yes, are there uncommitted changes to it?

3. If yes to both, can they merge cleanly, or refuse?

Why: this three-step decision runs independently for every file in the repo.
items.learnMore:
Per-file, not per-repo

Checkout's decision process runs independently for each file — a repo with 10,000 files might have only 3 files that actually differ between two branches, and checkout only touches those 3.

Common mistake

Thinking of checkout as one all-or-nothing operation on the whole working tree, rather than a per-file decision.

items.prompt: A repo has 10,000 files. Switching branches only actually updates 3 of them. Why so few?
choices: Git is broken and silently skipped the rest
Checkout only touches files whose content actually differs between the current and target commits — the other 9,997 are identical, so there's nothing to update
Git has a file-count limit per checkout
The other files were deleted
items.explanation: This is the per-file nature of checkout: it's fundamentally efficient (and predictable) because it skips every file that hasn't changed between the two commits, only touching the ones that actually differ.
items.reference:
1. Does the file differ between commits?

2. If yes, are there uncommitted changes to it?

3. If yes to both, can they merge cleanly, or refuse?

Why: this three-step decision runs independently for every file in the repo.

items.prompt: In L2/L3's Case 1 (silent carry-over) vs. Case 2 (refused), what's the ONE fact that differs between them?
choices: Whether `git status` was run before switching
Whether the target branch's committed version of the file genuinely differs from the current branch's committed version
Whether the edit was large or small
Whether the developer used `git checkout` vs `git switch`
items.explanation: Everything else in both cases was identical (an uncommitted edit, then a branch switch) — the only variable that changed the outcome was whether the target branch's committed content for that file actually diverged from the source branch's.
items.reference:
CaseFile differs in target?Outcome
1NoSilent carry-over
2YesRefused

Why: the presence of an uncommitted edit was identical in both cases — only target-branch divergence differed.
items.learnMore:
One variable, two outcomes

Isolating exactly which variable changes the outcome is the core diagnostic skill this unit builds — it's the difference between 'checkout is unpredictable' and 'checkout is fully deterministic, once you know what it checks.'

Common mistake

Concluding checkout's behavior is inconsistent or unpredictable, rather than identifying the specific condition that determines the outcome.

items.prompt: Why might a developer be MORE likely to lose track of an edit in Case 1 (silent success) than in Case 2 (refused)?
choices: Case 1 is actually less likely to happen in practice
Case 2 forces an explicit decision (commit, stash, or abort) right when it matters; Case 1 gives no signal at all that the edit's context has shifted to a different branch
Case 1 always deletes the file immediately
There's no meaningful difference in risk between the two cases
items.explanation: Case 2's error message is an unavoidable prompt to deal with the edit right then. Case 1 gives no such prompt — the developer can go on working, forget the edit exists, and only discover the problem much later, exactly as in L3's incident.

items.prompt: What would have prevented L3's incident, without changing which Git commands were available?
choices: Never using `git restore` or `git checkout -- .` under any circumstances
Committing (even as a throwaway "wip" commit) or stashing the edit before switching branches at all, so it's no longer sitting unprotected in the shared working tree
Always working on a single branch forever
Renaming the file before switching branches
items.explanation: Committing or stashing moves the edit into the repository or a dedicated stash entry — both are protected from a `restore`/`checkout --`/`reset --hard` run on a DIFFERENT branch, unlike the working tree, which has no per-branch memory.
items.reference:
The fix

`git commit -m "wip"` or `git stash` BEFORE switching branches with uncommitted work.

Why: both move the edit out of the shared, unprotected working tree.
items.learnMore:
A habit, not a different tool

The fix here isn't avoiding any Git command — restore, checkout --, and reset --hard are all legitimate, useful tools. The fix is a habit: before switching branches with uncommitted work in progress, decide whether that work needs to be protected (committed/stashed) first.

Common mistake

Avoiding useful discard commands entirely out of fear, instead of building the habit of checking git status before running one.

items.prompt: Why does stashing an edit protect it from a `git restore .` run on a different branch, when the working tree alone doesn't?
choices: Stashing doesn't actually protect anything — it's equally at risk
A stash entry is stored separately from the working tree, in its own list — `restore`/`checkout --` only ever touch the working tree, not the stash
Stashing automatically commits the change permanently
Stashing deletes the file entirely, so there's nothing left to lose
items.explanation: `git stash` moves the edit into a dedicated stash list, entirely separate from the working tree that `restore`/`checkout --` operate on — this is precisely why stashing (or committing) is protected where a bare uncommitted edit isn't.
items.reference:
The fix

`git commit -m "wip"` or `git stash` BEFORE switching branches with uncommitted work.

Why: both move the edit out of the shared, unprotected working tree.
items.learnMore:
A habit, not a different tool

The fix here isn't avoiding any Git command — restore, checkout --, and reset --hard are all legitimate, useful tools. The fix is a habit: before switching branches with uncommitted work in progress, decide whether that work needs to be protected (committed/stashed) first.

Common mistake

Avoiding useful discard commands entirely out of fear, instead of building the habit of checking git status before running one.

items.prompt: Implement `checkoutOutcome({ fileDiffersInTarget, hasUncommittedChange })`, modeling checkout's per-file decision from L2/L3: no uncommitted change + file differs → `'overwritten-from-target'`; no uncommitted change + file same → `'unchanged'`; uncommitted change + file same → `'carried-over'`; uncommitted change + file differs → `'refused'`.

tests.description: Case 1 from L3: identical file, uncommitted edit -> carried over
Case 2 from L3: diverged file, uncommitted edit -> refused
diverged file, no uncommitted edit -> overwritten from target
identical file, no uncommitted edit -> unchanged

items.explanation: This directly encodes L2's flowchart and reproduces both real transcripts from L3 — 'carried-over' matches Case 1's silent success, 'refused' matches Case 2's error, verified against the actual git behavior demonstrated in the unit.

items.prompt: Implement `checkoutOutcome({ fileDiffersInTarget, hasUncommittedChange })` (same rules). Verify that whether the file differs is IRRELEVANT when there's no uncommitted change of your own — the outcome only depends on the target's content in that case.

tests.description: no uncommitted change, file differs
no uncommitted change, file identical

items.explanation: Without an uncommitted change to protect, checkout has nothing risky to do either way — it simply syncs the working tree to whatever the target commit says, which is the normal, expected behavior of switching branches.

items.prompt: Implement `checkoutOutcome({ fileDiffersInTarget, hasUncommittedChange })` (same rules). Confirm 'refused' is the ONLY outcome that requires BOTH conditions to be true simultaneously.

tests.description: both true is the only path to refused
flipping either condition changes the outcome away from refused

items.explanation: This is the precise condition that separates L3's two cases: only when there's real work at risk (uncommitted change) AND real conflict potential (target differs) does Git step in and refuse — either condition alone is considered safe to proceed.

items.prompt: Implement `statusLabels({ workingTreeDiffersFromIndex, indexDiffersFromHead })`, modeling `git status`'s two independent diffs from L2. Return an array containing `'changes to be committed'` (if index differs from HEAD) and/or `'changes not staged for commit'` (if working tree differs from index), in that order, or an empty array if neither.

tests.description: no differences at all
only unstaged changes
tests.expr: expect(statusLabels({ workingTreeDiffersFromIndex: true, indexDiffersFromHead: false })).toEqual(['changes not staged for commit'])

tests.description: only staged changes
tests.expr: expect(statusLabels({ workingTreeDiffersFromIndex: false, indexDiffersFromHead: true })).toEqual(['changes to be committed'])

tests.description: both at once (edited after staging)
tests.expr: expect(statusLabels({ workingTreeDiffersFromIndex: true, indexDiffersFromHead: true })).toEqual(['changes to be committed', 'changes not staged for commit'])

items.explanation: This is L2's two-diff model made literal: the two conditions are checked completely independently, which is exactly why a file can appear under both status categories simultaneously — a real, common state most developers eventually hit.

items.prompt: Implement `statusLabels({ workingTreeDiffersFromIndex, indexDiffersFromHead })` (same rules). Verify the 'edit after staging' scenario from L2 — stage a change, then edit again — produces both labels.

tests.description: edit-after-staging produces both labels in the documented order
tests.expr: expect(statusLabels({ workingTreeDiffersFromIndex: true, indexDiffersFromHead: true })[0]).toBe('changes to be committed')

tests.description: second label is the unstaged one
tests.expr: expect(statusLabels({ workingTreeDiffersFromIndex: true, indexDiffersFromHead: true })[1]).toBe('changes not staged for commit')

items.explanation: This is exactly L2's 'you `git add` a file, then edit it again' scenario — the staged content differs from HEAD (staged changes exist), and the working tree now differs from that staged snapshot too (a further unstaged edit on top).

items.prompt: Implement `filesAtRisk(files)` — `files` is an array of `{ name, hasUncommittedChange, differsInTarget }`. Return the names of files where a checkout would be REFUSED (both flags true).

tests.description: only the file matching both conditions is at risk
tests.expr: expect(filesAtRisk([{ name: 'a.js', hasUncommittedChange: true, differsInTarget: true }, { name: 'b.js', hasUncommittedChange: true, differsInTarget: false }])).toEqual(['a.js'])

tests.description: no files at risk
tests.expr: expect(filesAtRisk([{ name: 'c.js', hasUncommittedChange: false, differsInTarget: true }])).toEqual([])

tests.description: empty input

items.explanation: This scales the single-file decision from `checkoutOutcome` to a whole checkout — since checkout evaluates every file independently, the set of at-risk files is simply every file matching both risk conditions at once.

items.prompt: Implement `filesAtRisk(files)` (same rules). Verify that a large repo with mostly-unmodified files still correctly identifies only the genuinely at-risk ones, matching L2's '3 out of 10,000 files' point.

tests.description: mixed set with only one genuinely at-risk file
tests.expr: expect(filesAtRisk([{ name: 'x', hasUncommittedChange: true, differsInTarget: true }, { name: 'y', hasUncommittedChange: false, differsInTarget: false }, { name: 'z', hasUncommittedChange: false, differsInTarget: true }])).toEqual(['x'])

items.explanation: Even with a mix of untouched, target-only-changed, and genuinely at-risk files, the filter correctly isolates only files where BOTH conditions hold — matching the exact 'refused' condition from checkoutOutcome, applied per-file across the whole repo.

items.prompt: Implement `isDiscardRecoverable({ wasEverCommitted })`. A discard command (`restore`, `checkout --`, `reset --hard`) is only recoverable (via reflog or a prior commit) if the content was committed at least once before being discarded. Return that boolean directly.

tests.description: content committed at least once is recoverable
content never committed is NOT recoverable

items.explanation: This mirrors this track's `checkout` unit's own reflog finding, applied to this unit's incident: reflog only tracks commits, never uncommitted working-tree content, so an edit like L3's — never staged, never committed — has no recovery path once discarded.

items.prompt: Implement `isDiscardRecoverable({ wasEverCommitted })` (same rules). Confirm it correctly classifies L3's specific incident as unrecoverable.

tests.description: L3's shared-config.js edit: never committed -> unrecoverable
a throwaway wip commit would have made the same edit recoverable

items.explanation: Applying this directly to L3's incident: `shared-config.js`'s edit was never staged or committed, so `wasEverCommitted` is false and the edit was genuinely, permanently unrecoverable the moment `git restore .` ran.

items.prompt: Implement `describeThreeAreas({ onDisk, staged, committed })` — three string 'versions' of a file. Return an array: `'changes to be committed'` if `staged !== committed`, `'changes not staged for commit'` if `onDisk !== staged`, or `['clean']` if neither differs.

tests.description: edited but not staged
tests.expr: expect(describeThreeAreas({ onDisk: 'v2', staged: 'v1', committed: 'v1' })).toEqual(['changes not staged for commit'])

tests.description: clean file, all three match
staged but not committed
tests.expr: expect(describeThreeAreas({ onDisk: 'v2', staged: 'v2', committed: 'v1' })).toEqual(['changes to be committed'])

items.explanation: This is L1's three-area table made concrete and testable — three independent string values standing in for a file's state in each area, compared pairwise exactly as git status does internally.

items.prompt: Implement `describeThreeAreas({ onDisk, staged, committed })` (same rules). Verify the 'edited twice' scenario from L2 (staged once, then edited again) produces both labels.

tests.description: edited after staging shows both labels
tests.expr: expect(describeThreeAreas({ onDisk: 'v3', staged: 'v2', committed: 'v1' })).toEqual(['changes to be committed', 'changes not staged for commit'])

items.explanation: With three genuinely different values (v1 committed, v2 staged, v3 on disk), both pairwise comparisons differ, producing both labels — the exact 'edited after staging' state from L2's status walkthrough.

items.prompt: Why does Git have a separate staging step (`git add`) instead of just committing whatever is currently in the working tree?
choices: It doesn't serve a real purpose — it's a legacy step that should be skipped with `commit -a`
Staging lets you build a commit out of only part of what you've edited — stage exactly the related changes, leave unrelated edits for a separate commit
Staging is required by Git for performance reasons only
Staging automatically writes a commit message for you
items.explanation: The staging area exists specifically to let you assemble a commit deliberately — including some edits and excluding others — rather than being forced to commit everything currently in the working tree at once.
items.reference:
Working tree — what you see and edit

Index/staging — a prepared snapshot, built deliberately

Why: staging is a deliberate, separate step, not an automatic side effect of editing.
items.learnMore:
Why a staging step at all

The index lets you build a commit out of only PART of what you've edited — stage exactly the lines/files that belong together, leave the rest for a later commit. Without a separate staging step, every commit would have to include everything currently edited, with no way to split unrelated changes apart.

Common mistake

Treating `git add` as a formality rather than a genuine, deliberate choice about what belongs in the next commit.

items.prompt: A developer has edited two unrelated files but only wants to commit one of them right now. What lets them do this?
choices: Nothing — Git always commits every edited file at once
Staging only the one file they want (`git add thatFile.js`), leaving the other edited-but-unstaged, so the commit only includes what was staged
Deleting the file they don't want to commit
Renaming the branch
items.explanation: Because `git commit` snapshots the index (not the whole working tree), staging only one file lets that commit include exactly that file, leaving the other edit sitting unstaged for later.
items.reference:

Why: staging is a deliberate, separate step, not an automatic side effect of editing.
items.learnMore:

items.prompt: What does the staging area/index actually represent?

A prepared, deliberately-assembled snapshot of exactly what the NEXT commit will contain
A list of file names only, with no content
A cache of remote branch names
items.explanation: The index holds real staged content — not just file names — representing precisely what `git commit` will record if run right now.

Why a staging step at all

The index lets you build a commit out of only PART of what you've edited — stage exactly the lines/files that belong together, leave the rest for a later commit. Without a separate staging step, every commit would have to include everything currently edited, with no way to split unrelated changes apart.

Common mistake

Treating `git add` as a formality rather than a genuine, deliberate choice about what belongs in the next commit.

items.prompt: `git add -p` lets you stage only SOME of the changed lines within a single file. What does this reveal about the index?
choices: It reveals nothing new — staging is always all-or-nothing per file
The index is a genuine, independently-chosen snapshot that can differ from the working tree at a finer granularity than 'whole file changed or not'

Why: the index can hold a different subset of a single file's edits than what's on disk.
items.learnMore:
Partial staging is real

`git add -p` lets you stage only some of the changed lines within a single file, leaving the rest unstaged — the index genuinely stores a distinct, independently-chosen snapshot, not merely a boolean flag on top of the working tree.

Common mistake

Assuming staging only works at whole-file granularity — hunk-level staging is a real, commonly used Git feature.

items.prompt: You create a brand-new file (never `git add`ed) on `feature-a`, then switch to `feature-b`. What happens to that new file?
choices: Git refuses the checkout, treating it like a tracked-file conflict
It stays exactly as-is — checkout only manages tracked files (ones existing in at least one commit), and an untracked file has no committed version anywhere to compare against
It gets silently deleted
It gets automatically committed to feature-a before the switch
items.explanation: Untracked files fall entirely outside checkout's per-file comparison, since that comparison is between committed versions — a never-added file was never in any commit, so it always just stays put.
items.reference:
Checkout only ever manages TRACKED files (files that exist in at least one commit).

A brand-new untracked file is simply never part of the comparison — it stays, unconditionally.

Why: checkout compares committed versions of files; an untracked file was never in any commit to compare.
items.learnMore:
Untracked files sit outside the whole model

Everything in L1-L3 about checkout's per-file decision applies specifically to TRACKED files (ones that exist in at least one commit). A brand-new, never-added file has no committed version on any branch to compare against, so checkout leaves it alone unconditionally — it neither refuses nor gets overwritten.

Common mistake

Assuming checkout's safety net (the refusal case) protects untracked files too — untracked files are outside that entire mechanism, for a different reason (they carry over unconditionally, not because of a safety check).

items.prompt: Why doesn't checkout's 'local changes would be overwritten' safety check apply to untracked files?
choices: It's a known bug that's never been fixed
That check compares a tracked file's committed versions across branches — an untracked file has no committed version at all, so there's nothing for the check to compare
Untracked files are always protected by a different, stronger check
The check does apply, contrary to what most developers believe
items.explanation: The refusal check specifically compares committed content between branches for a given path — since an untracked file was never committed anywhere, that comparison simply doesn't apply to it, so it's unconditionally left alone instead.
